tagline: The railroad left; the charcoal kilns remained.
intro: From Fort Bridger the backway takes gravel county roads south and west to Muddy Creek, one of the famous camps of the western migration. The water was good and the bunchgrass grew tall, and some 70,000 Mormon pioneers crossed, passed through or camped here. A stage stop and a Pony Express station followed.

Piedmont, at the end, cut ties and burned charcoal for the railroad until the Union Pacific bored a tunnel through Aspen Mountain and rerouted the line several miles away. The road ends at the ghost town, where three beehive kilns of local sandstone have outlasted it.

moments.title: Fort Bridger
moments.text: The backway starts on WY 219 in the town that took its name from Jim Bridger's trading post.

moments.title: Muddy Creek
moments.text: Brigham Young's first company of Mormon pioneers used this campsite in the summer of 1847, and 2,000 army men camped here in June 1858.

moments.title: Piedmont Charcoal Kilns
moments.text: Moses Byrne built five kilns here to make charcoal for smelters and blacksmith shops in the Salt Lake Valley; three still stand, about 30 feet high.

practical: The roads are gravel and may not suit travel in adverse weather; the remains of Piedmont are on private property, while the kilns are a state historic site.
